compositions.title: Food and water for the journey
compositions.text: Se mann cwæð: ‘Ic wille faran. Mīn scip is gearu. Cumað and helpað mē.’ Twēgen gefēran cōmon tō helpanne. Se mann cwæð: ‘Nimað ðone męte and berað hine. Giefað ðǣm fuglum ðæt wæter.’ Se gefēra cwæð: ‘Ic mæg ðone męte beran. Wē sculon ðæt weorc gefręmman.’ Ðā gefēran bǣron ðone męte and gēafon ðǣm fuglum ðæt wæter. Se mann cwæð: ‘Sittað and etað.’ Ðā gefēran ǣton. Hīe fōron.
compositions.intended_meaning: The man said: ‘I want to travel. My ship is ready. Come and help me.’ Two companions came to help. The man said: ‘Take the food and carry it. Give the birds the water.’ The companion said: ‘I can carry the food. We must perform the work.’ The companions carried the food and gave the birds the water. The man said: ‘Sit and eat.’ The companions ate. They travelled.
audit_requests: Verify complete imperative pairs for cuman, helpan, niman, beran, giefan, sittan and etan; the passage uses the plural cells.
Verify tō helpanne as purposive inflected infinitive with the same human subject as cōmon; no indirect-question or content clause.
Verify willan+faran for volition, magan+beran for physical ability and sculan+gefręmman for obligation.
Extend taught cweðan direct quotation explicitly to taught commands; prior indicative quotation alone does not cover these.
All ordinary lexical arguments and nouns are earlier taught: accusative food/water, dative help-recipient and gift-recipient; grammatical reference hine to masculine męte.
The final plural hīe can include the participants contextually; a question should not demand a uniquely encoded antecedent.
Assess naturalness: the birds receive the water, the companions receive the food, and the journey follows their meal. No new directional phrase or purpose of the ship is asserted.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Learned ability, present singular/plural; plain infinitives.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Present ability; accusative carried object and dative helped person.
candidate_sequences: Hē mæg ðæt wæter beran. Hīe magon ðǣm męnn helpan.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “I need to go. We needed to go.” Use ðurfan.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Need with a plain infinitive; present and preterite.
candidate_sequences: Ic ðearf gān. Wē ðorfton gān.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “You dare to go. You dared to go.” Address one person and use durran.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Daring with a plain infinitive and explicit second-person singular.
candidate_sequences: Ðū dearst gān. Ðū dorstest gān.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “We must do the work. They had to do the work.” Use sculan for obligation.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Present and past obligation, not future or conditional projection.
candidate_sequences: Wē sculon ðæt weorc dōn. Hīe sceoldon ðæt weorc dōn.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “You are allowed to eat the food. You were allowed to eat the food.” Address one person and use mōtan.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Present and past permission; modal sense must be evidence-checked.
candidate_sequences: Ðū mōst ðone męte etan. Ðū mōstest ðone męte etan.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “He wants to give the birds water. They wanted to give the birds water.” Use willan for desire.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Volition with plain infinitive and prior giving frame.
candidate_sequences: Hē wille ðǣm fuglum wæter giefan. Hīe woldon ðǣm fuglum wæter giefan.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “I did not dare to go. We cannot carry the ship.” Use the taught simple ne construction.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Simple negation with audited irregular indicative systems; no negative concord or new contracted forms.
candidate_sequences: Ic ne dorste gān. Wē ne magon ðæt scip beran.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “We two know how to swim. You two must help us two.” Keep the two-person references.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Dual pronoun subjects with plural modal verbs and dative dual helped recipients.
candidate_sequences: Wit cunnon swimman. Git sculon unc helpan.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “He wanted to go. He went.” Explain why the first sentence alone does not assert that he went.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Volition distinguished from fulfilled motion, not mechanical future-in-the-past.
candidate_sequences: Hē wolde gān. Hē ēode.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate the printed pairs Ic cann swimman and Ic mæg swimman using the unit’s stated difference between learned ability and present capability. Identify the finite verb and the infinitive in each. Do not claim that one English word always represents only one Old English modal.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Bounded modal contrast and finite versus nonfinite roles.
candidate_sequences: Ic cann swimman. Ic mæg swimman.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “The ship will be ready.” Use the bēo-series indicative to describe the expected later state. Then contrast the earlier eom-series sentence “The ship is ready.” Do not infer that every bēo-series occurrence must be future.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Elementary future-state bēon use with prior neuter predicate-adjective agreement; distinguish an assigned use from a universal tense rule.
candidate_sequences: Ðæt scip bið gearu. Ðæt scip is gearu.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: The “things” here are matters already discussed. Translate “I know those things. He knew those things.” Use witan. Explain how this knowledge construction differs from cunnan followed by an infinitive.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Present/past knowledge with an accusative nominal object and the prior pointing demonstrative; distinct from learned ability plus an infinitive.
candidate_sequences: Ic wāt ðā ðing. Hē wiste ðā ðing.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “Take the food and carry it.” First address one person, then several. Identify what “it” refers to and preserve its grammatical gender.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Singular/plural commands with masculine accusative pronoun reference.
candidate_sequences: Nim ðone męte and ber hine. Nimað ðone męte and berað hine.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “Help me. Give me the water.” First address one person, then exactly two people. Explain the verb number used for the two addressees.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Dative recipients with singular and plural imperative; no invented dual imperative ending.
candidate_sequences: Help mē. Gief mē ðæt wæter. Helpað mē. Giefað mē ðæt wæter.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “Do not drink the water. Sit and eat.” Address several people.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Elementary negative command followed by coordinated positive plural commands.
candidate_sequences: Ne drincað ðæt wæter. Sittað and etað.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “The man said: ‘Go and do the work well.’” The man addresses one companion.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Prior cweðan quotation extended to direct commands; anomalous imperatives and prior manner adverb.
candidate_sequences: Se mann cwæð: ‘Gā and dō ðæt weorc wel.’

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “He wants to eat. He came to eat.” Use the taught plain-infinitive complement in the first sentence and the taught purpose construction in the second.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Plain versus tō+inflected infinitive; no added subordinate finite mood.
candidate_sequences: Hē wille etan. Hē cōm tō etanne.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “The companions came to help the man.” Use the inflected infinitive for their purpose. Identify the person doing the helping and the case of the person helped.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Same-subject purpose after cuman with the prior dative help-frame; distinguish a valid bare-purpose alternative from this expressly requested inflected target.
candidate_sequences: Ðā gefēran cōmon tō helpanne ðǣm męnn.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “The man came to give food to the birds.” Use the inflected infinitive for the purpose.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Purpose with a transitive infinitive and dative recipient.
candidate_sequences: Se mann cōm tō giefanne męte ðǣm fuglum.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: In Hīe sculon ðæt weorc dōn and Hīe cōmon tō dōnne ðæt weorc, identify each finite verb, each infinitive, and the construction that selects the infinitive form. Translate both sentences.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Modal complement versus purpose, with anomalous infinitive stem.
candidate_sequences: Hīe sculon ðæt weorc dōn. Hīe cōmon tō dōnne ðæt weorc.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Complete the taught modal construction “We can carry the food” using mugan and beran. Then make the subject “I”. Explain which verb changes for person and number.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Only the finite modal agrees; the plain infinitive remains unchanged.
candidate_sequences: Wē magon ðone męte beran. Ic mæg ðone męte beran.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Rewrite the man’s first quoted commands, Cumað and helpað mē, as commands to one companion. Then put the first sentence of the narrative into the present, keeping the quotation itself unchanged.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Number adjustment in commands and finite narrative-tense adjustment with stable quotation.
candidate_sequences: Cum and help mē. Se mann cwið: ‘Ic wille faran. Mīn scip is gearu. Cumað and helpað mē.’

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “We two wanted to give our food to the birds. We two gave it to them.” Retain the two-person possessor and the grammatical gender of “food”.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Cumulative dual reference, agreeing possessive, volitional infinitive, past giving and anaphora.
candidate_sequences: Wit woldon uncerne męte ðǣm fuglum giefan. Wit gēafon hine him.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “The old man cannot carry the great ship. Help him.” Address several companions in the command.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Weak attributive adjectives, modal negation, accusative object and dative help-recipient.
candidate_sequences: Se ealda mann ne mæg ðæt micle scip beran. Helpað him.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Translate “He came to help us. We wanted to give him food. He sat and ate.” Use the taught elementary purpose and volitional constructions.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Purpose, desire, dative recipients and completed indicative actions.
candidate_sequences: Hē cōm tō helpanne ūs. Wē woldon him męte giefan. Hē sæt and ǣt.

tasks_with_candidate_sequences.prompt: Compare the statement Gē gāð with the command Gāð. Explain the shared spelling and the difference in use. Then compare Hē dēð ðæt weorc with Dō ðæt weorc.
tasks_with_candidate_sequences.target_specification: Syncretism does not erase mood/use distinctions; singular imperative differs from indicative3sg.
candidate_sequences: Gē gāð. Gāð. Hē dēð ðæt weorc. Dō ðæt weorc.
